Welcome to the Reverse Engineering module! In this lesson, you will learn how to extract hidden information from Android applications.

• APKTool - Decompiles APK files
• Jadx - Java decompiler
• dex2jar - Converts DEX to JAR
• JD-GUI - Java class viewer
• Android Studio - APK Analyzer

1. Static Analysis - Examine code without running
2. String Search - Look for hardcoded values
3. Network Analysis - Monitor API calls
4. Decompilation - Convert bytecode to source

• Check strings.xml for hardcoded text
• Look in BuildConfig and resource files
• Examine obfuscated code carefully
• Use grep to search decompiled code
• Check native libraries (.so files)
Find the flag hidden in plain sight within this application. Use static analysis tools to decompile the APK and search through the code.
Hint: The flag is stored as a simple string constant in one of the Java classes. Try searching for "flag" or "key" in the decompiled code.
This flag has been encoded to make it slightly harder to find. You\'ll need to decode it after finding it in the source code.
Hint: Look for Base64 encoded strings or other common encoding schemes. The flag might be split across multiple variables or methods.
That\'s not right. Check your decoding.
The hardest challenge yet! The flag is obfuscated and split across multiple locations. You\'ll need advanced reverse engineering skills.
Hint: The flag is constructed at runtime using multiple obfuscated methods. Look for string concatenation, XOR operations, or reflection. Try debugging or analyzing the bytecode.

Learn about insecure data storage vulnerabilities in mobile applications. This is one of the most common security issues in mobile apps where sensitive information is stored without proper protection.

Insecure data storage occurs when sensitive information like passwords, tokens, personal data, or cryptographic keys are stored on the device without adequate protection. Attackers with physical access to the device or malware can extract this data.

• SQLite Databases (unencrypted)
• SharedPreferences (plain text)
• Internal Storage files
• External Storage (SD card)
• Application logs
• Temporary files
• Cloud storage backups

1. Physical Access - Anyone with the device can extract data
2. Backup Exposure - Data in cloud backups
3. Malware - Other apps can access unprotected data
4. Forensics - Data persists even after app deletion
5. Rooted Devices - Full filesystem access

• Use ADB to pull app data directory
• Examine SQLite databases with sqlite3
• Check SharedPreferences XML files
• Review app logs with logcat
• Use tools like Objection or Frida
• Inspect backup files
WARNING: This is an intentionally vulnerable mobile application!

This app is part of the OWASP Security Shepherd Project - a web and mobile application security training platform.

Security Shepherd is designed to foster and improve security awareness among a varied skill-set demographic. The aim is to educate users about application security through hands-on challenges.

This mobile app contains intentional security vulnerabilities for educational purposes. Do NOT install this on a device with sensitive data.

This challenge stores a password hash in a SQLite database. Unlike simple encoding, this password has been hashed using MD5. Your task is to crack the hash and recover the original password.\n\nThe key is not in the UI - crack the hash!

1. Extract the passwordDB.db database using ADB
2. The password is stored as an MD5 hash
3. MD5 is a weak hashing algorithm
4. Use online rainbow tables or tools like hashcat
5. Hash: 0e3a0c8c3a571a855c958813d9b851a1

Step-by-Step Guide:

1. EXTRACT THE APK
 • Connect device via ADB
 • Run: adb shell pm list packages | grep reverser
 • Run: adb shell pm path com.owasp.app
 • Run: adb pull /data/app/[path]/base.apk

2. DECOMPILE WITH JADX
 • Download JADX from GitHub
 • Run: jadx base.apk
 • Or use JADX-GUI for visual interface

3. NAVIGATE TO TARGET FILE
 • Open: sources/com/owasp/reverser/ui/lessons/LessonFragment.java
 • Look in the class body for string variables
 • Search for keywords: flag, key, secret, password

4. ALTERNATIVE TOOLS
 • APKTool: apktool d base.apk (produces smali)
 • dex2jar + JD-GUI: For JAR decompilation
 • Ghidra: Advanced static analysis
 • Frida: Dynamic runtime inspection

5. WHAT TO LOOK FOR
 • Hardcoded strings in class fields
 • Static final String variables
 • Suspicious base64 or hex strings
 • Comments or debug messages

Target: LessonFragment.java in package com.owasp.app.ui.lessons
Check logcat for debugging information about hardcoded credentials and authentication logic.
Check logcat for third-party library initialization messages that may reveal hardcoded credentials or API keys.
Monitor logcat with tag \'NetworkTraffic\' while clicking Send to see plaintext HTTP traffic including credentials.

This challenge stores sensitive credentials in Android SharedPreferences. Many developers think this is secure, but SharedPreferences files are stored as plain XML and can be easily extracted.\n\nYour mission: Extract the SharedPreferences XML file and find the secret flag among the stored credentials.

1. Use ADB to pull SharedPreferences files
2. Location: /data/data/com.owasp.app/shared_prefs/
3. File name: UserCredentials.xml
4. SharedPreferences stores everything in plain text XML
5. Look for a key named "secret_flag"
6. Command: adb pull /data/data/com.owasp.app/shared_prefs/UserCredentials.xml

This challenge implements custom encryption using a XOR cipher. While the data appears encrypted, the encryption scheme is weak and can be reverse engineered.\n\nYour mission: Decompile the APK, analyze the encryption algorithm, and decrypt the flag. This challenge requires understanding of cryptographic weaknesses.

1. Decompile the APK using jadx or apktool
2. Find the InsecureData3Fragment class
3. Analyze the xorEncrypt() method
4. The XOR key is hardcoded as "SHEPHERD"
5. XOR is symmetric - encryption and decryption are identical
6. Use the encrypted hex data shown in the app
7. Decrypt: ciphertext XOR key = plaintext
Poor authentication is one of the most critical mobile vulnerabilities. Authentication is the cornerstone of app security - if attackers bypass it, all other security measures become irrelevant.

• Weak security questions (easily guessable)
• Passwords logged in plaintext
• Credentials in world-readable files
• Weak temporary passwords
• Verbose error messages
• Debug logs in production

Why Security Questions Fail:

• Answers often public (social media)
• Easy to guess or research
• Predictable common answers
• Never change over time

Better Alternatives:
• Email-based password reset
• SMS one-time codes
• Biometric authentication

Logging Dangers:

• Logcat accessible via ADB
• World-readable files
• Logs persist after deletion
• Cloud backups expose data

Never Log:
• Passwords, PINs, tokens
• API keys
• Personal information
• Security answers

Secure Practices:

• Strong password policies
• Multi-factor authentication
• Email verification for resets
• Account lockout after failures
• Never log credentials
• Disable debug logs in production

This challenge covers multiple poor authentication vulnerabilities:

• Weak security questions with easily discoverable answers
• Sensitive information logged to logcat
• Personal details written to files
• Weak temporary password generation

Your mission: The account is locked, but you can use the password reset feature. Find the security question answers by examining logs and files, reset the password, login, and capture the flag!

Hint: Start by checking logcat for interesting information...

Insecure authorization occurs when apps fail to properly enforce access controls after authentication. Even if users authenticate correctly, improper authorization checks allow privilege escalation, accessing other users\' data, or performing unauthorized actions. This lesson demonstrates client-side authorization flaws where role/permission checks can be manipulated.

Inadequate supply chain security occurs when mobile apps use vulnerable third-party libraries, SDKs, or dependencies. Attackers exploit these weak links to compromise entire applications, affecting millions of users.

Third-Party Risks:

• Outdated libraries with known CVEs
• Malicious code in dependencies
• Hardcoded credentials in SDKs
• Unvetted third-party components
• Supply chain attacks (compromised updates)
• Backdoors in vendor libraries

Common Issues:

• Using dependencies with known vulnerabilities
• Not verifying SDK authenticity
• Hardcoded API keys in libraries
• Insecure data collection by third parties
• Excessive permissions requested by SDKs
• Outdated dependencies not updated for years

Secure Practices:

• Regularly audit and update dependencies
• Use dependency scanning tools (OWASP Dependency-Check)
• Verify checksums and signatures
• Monitor CVE databases
• Remove unused dependencies
• Review third-party SDK permissions
• Implement secure update mechanisms
• Use Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)

This app uses a vulnerable third-party analytics SDK from "ThirdPartyAnalytics Inc." The SDK is severely outdated (16 months old) and contains multiple security issues:

• Known CVEs (CVE-2023-45678, CVE-2024-12345)
• Hardcoded backdoor authentication token
• Insecure telemetry data storage
• Base64-encoded credentials in logs

Your mission: Analyze the SDK initialization process, examine logcat logs, inspect the app's files directory, and find the hidden flag that proves you've successfully exploited the supply chain vulnerability!

Hint: Use logcat filtering and explore the app's data directory using Device File Explorer or ADB.

Insecure communication occurs when mobile apps transmit sensitive data without proper encryption. Any attacker on the same network can intercept, read, and modify unencrypted traffic, leading to credential theft, session hijacking, and data breaches.

HTTP vs HTTPS:

• HTTP: Plaintext protocol - all data visible to anyone monitoring the network
• HTTPS: Encrypted with TLS/SSL - protects data confidentiality and integrity
• Mixed content: Using both HTTP and HTTPS exposes users to attacks
• Certificate validation: Must verify server identity to prevent MITM attacks

Common Issues:

• Sending credentials over HTTP
• Accepting invalid/self-signed certificates
• Using weak cipher suites or deprecated TLS versions
• Disabling certificate pinning for convenience
• Sensitive data in URLs (visible in logs/history)
• Mixed HTTP/HTTPS sessions exposing session tokens

Secure Practices:

• Always use HTTPS for all network communications
• Validate SSL/TLS certificates properly
• Implement certificate pinning for critical APIs
• Use strong cipher suites (TLS 1.2+)
• Never disable certificate validation in production
• Keep sensitive data out of URLs
• Use secure WebSocket (WSS) for real-time communication

This app makes multiple network requests to different endpoints. Some use HTTPS (secure), while others use HTTP (insecure).

Your mission: Monitor the app's network traffic using logcat, identify which requests are sent over HTTP, and extract the session token that was transmitted in plaintext.

Hints:
• Use logcat filter tag: AppNetworkMonitor
• Look for HTTP (not HTTPS) requests
• The flag is in the X-Session-Token header
• Pay attention to protocol warnings

Insufficient cryptography occurs when mobile apps use weak encryption algorithms, inadequate key lengths, poor key management, or flawed cryptographic implementations. These weaknesses allow attackers to decrypt sensitive data, bypass encryption, or manipulate cryptographic processes.

Common Crypto Vulnerabilities:

• Weak algorithms: DES, RC4, MD5, SHA-1
• Insufficient key length: Keys < 128 bits
• ECB mode: Pattern analysis attacks
• Hardcoded keys: Keys in source code
• Static IVs: Initialization vector reuse
• Weak key derivation: Simple hashing for keys
• Insecure random: Predictable Random() instead of SecureRandom
• No salt: Password hashing without random salt

Secure Cryptography Practices:

• Use AES-256 for symmetric encryption
• Use RSA-2048+ or ECC for asymmetric crypto
• Always use CBC, CTR, or GCM mode (never ECB)
• Generate random IVs for each encryption
• Use SecureRandom for all cryptographic values
• Store keys in Android Keystore
• Use PBKDF2, bcrypt, or scrypt for key derivation
• Always salt password hashes
• Use SHA-256 or SHA-3 for hashing
• Implement proper key rotation
• Never hardcode cryptographic keys

Real-World Consequences:

• Data Breaches: Encrypted data exposed when weak crypto is cracked
• Compliance Violations: GDPR, PCI-DSS require strong encryption
• Financial Loss: Credit card theft, fraud from decrypted data
• Reputation Damage: Loss of customer trust
• Intellectual Property Theft: Competitors access proprietary algorithms

Example: In 2019, a banking app used DES encryption. Researchers cracked it in 6 hours, exposing millions of customer accounts.

This app implements cryptographic operations with multiple severe vulnerabilities:

• ECB Mode: Electronic Codebook mode reveals patterns in encrypted data
• MD5 Key Derivation: Using broken MD5 hash to generate encryption keys
• Insecure Random: Predictable Random() with fixed seed instead of SecureRandom
• Static IV: Reusing the same Initialization Vector for all encryptions

Your mission: Analyze the cryptographic implementation by monitoring logcat logs, decompile the APK to examine the crypto code, identify all vulnerabilities, and extract the hidden flag!

Hints:
• Filter logcat with tag: InsufficientCryptoChallenge
• Look for cipher suite, key derivation method, IV usage
• Use jadx to decompile and search for crypto-related classes
• The flag is obfuscated in byte arrays in the source code

Security misconfiguration occurs when security settings are not properly defined, implemented, maintained, or enforced. This is one of the most common vulnerabilities in mobile applications, often resulting from default configurations, incomplete setups, or overly permissive settings that expose the app to various attack vectors.

Common Security Misconfigurations:

• Debug Mode Enabled: android:debuggable=true allows JDWP debugging in production
• Backup Allowed: android:allowBackup=true enables ADB backup extraction of app data
• Exported Components: Activities/Services/Receivers without proper permission checks
• Cleartext Traffic: Allowing unencrypted HTTP connections
• Excessive Permissions: Requesting unnecessary dangerous permissions
• Verbose Error Messages: Leaking sensitive information in production logs
• Default Credentials: Unchanged API keys, passwords in configuration files
• Insecure File Permissions: World-readable/writable files
• Missing Certificate Pinning: Vulnerable to MITM attacks
• WebView Misconfigurations: JavaScript enabled, file access allowed

Secure Configuration Best Practices:

• Always set android:debuggable=false for production builds
• Disable backup or use encrypted backups (android:allowBackup=false)
• Require permissions for all exported components
• Enforce HTTPS-only with Network Security Config
• Follow principle of least privilege for permissions
• Disable verbose logging in production builds
• Remove or secure default credentials and test accounts
• Use proper file permissions (MODE_PRIVATE)
• Implement certificate pinning for sensitive connections
• Regular security audits and configuration reviews
• Use build variants to manage debug vs release configurations
• Implement ProGuard/R8 obfuscation
• Sign APKs with strong keys and store securely

Attack Scenarios:

• Debug Mode: Attacker debugs app, inspects memory, modifies runtime behavior
• Backup Extraction: Use adb backup to extract SharedPreferences, databases with sensitive data
• Exported Components: Launch activities/services via ADB intents to bypass authentication
• Cleartext Traffic: MITM attack intercepts HTTP API calls, steals tokens
• Verbose Logs: Logcat reveals API keys, user credentials, session tokens
• Default Credentials: Access admin panels, internal APIs with known credentials

Real Impact: In 2020, a popular banking app had debuggable=true in production, allowing attackers to extract encryption keys from memory and decrypt user data.

This application has backup enabled (android:allowBackup="true"), allowing app data to be extracted using Android Debug Bridge.

Your mission: Use ADB to create a backup of this app's data, extract the backup file, and find the flag stored in SharedPreferences.

Steps:
1. Create backup: adb backup -f backup.ab -noapk com.owasp.app
2. Convert .ab to .tar: Use abe.jar or android-backup-extractor
3. Extract tar: tar -xvf backup.tar
4. Find SharedPreferences XML files
5. Locate the flag in the preferences

The flag is stored in plain text in the SharedPreferences!

This application has a SecretActivity that is exported without proper permission checks, allowing it to be launched directly via ADB or by other applications.

Your mission: Find the exported activity in AndroidManifest.xml and launch it with the correct intent extras to reveal the flag.

Steps:
1. Decompile APK or read AndroidManifest.xml
2. Find the exported activity (android:exported="true")
3. Identify required intent extras from challenge hints
4. Launch via ADB: adb shell am start -n com.owasp.app/.SecretActivity -e unlock_code shepherd2023
5. The activity will display the flag when launched correctly

This shows how exported components without authentication can be exploited!

Input/Output validation vulnerabilities occur when applications fail to properly validate, sanitize, or encode data at trust boundaries. This includes both data coming into the app (user input, API responses, intents) and data going out (WebView content, logs, broadcasts). Insufficient validation can lead to injection attacks, data corruption, security bypasses, and unintended application behavior.

Common Input/Output Validation Issues:

• SQL Injection: Unsanitized input in database queries allows data extraction
• Path Traversal: Unvalidated file paths enable access to unauthorized files
• WebView XSS: Unescaped user data rendered in WebViews enables script injection
• Intent Injection: Malicious data in Android Intents bypasses security checks
• Command Injection: User input passed to system commands enables arbitrary execution
• XML/JSON Injection: Malformed data breaks parsers and logic
• Log Injection: Unvalidated data in logs creates fake entries or leaks data
• URL Validation Bypass: Weak URL checks allow access to unauthorized resources
• Format String Attacks: User input in format strings causes crashes or leaks
• Deep Link Exploits: Improperly validated deep link parameters bypass authentication

URL Validation Bypass Techniques:

The lesson demonstrates a common URL validation flaw where the app checks if a trusted domain appears ANYWHERE in the URL using contains().

Bypass Methods:
1. Subdomain: https://example.com.evil.com
2. Parameter: https://evil.com?redirect=example.com
3. Fragment: https://evil.com#example.com
4. Path: https://evil.com/example.com
5. Username: https://example.com@evil.com

Proper Validation:
• Use startsWith() for protocol + domain
• Parse URL and check host property
• Use allowlist of exact domains
• Validate scheme (https only)
• Check against URL.getHost() not full URL string

Try these payloads:
• https://evil.com?trusted=example.com
• https://example.com.attacker.com
• https://malicious.com#example.com

The flag reveals when you successfully bypass the validation!
Learn how image metadata can leak sensitive information about users, including location, device info, and timestamps. This lesson demonstrates OWASP Mobile Top 10 M6: Inadequate Privacy Controls.
Load the sample image and analyze its metadata to find the hidden flag. Pay attention to EXIF data that applications often fail to strip before sharing or uploading images.

Photos taken by mobile devices contain extensive metadata (EXIF) that can reveal:
• GPS coordinates (exact location)
• Device make and model
• Timestamp when photo was taken
• Software/app used
• Camera settings
• User comments and descriptions

Most apps fail to strip this data before sharing!
No image loaded. Tap \"Load Sample Image\" to begin.

Inadequate Privacy Controls occur when mobile applications fail to properly handle user data privacy. This includes:

• Not stripping metadata from photos/videos before sharing
• Leaking location data through EXIF tags
• Failing to anonymize personal information
• Excessive data collection without user consent
• Storing sensitive data in accessible locations
• Transmitting PII without encryption
• Not respecting privacy settings

This vulnerability is classified as OWASP Mobile Top 10 M6.

Privacy Control Failures:

• Image Metadata Leakage: Photos contain GPS coordinates, timestamps, device info in EXIF data
• Location Tracking: Apps collect precise location without clear user benefit
• Clipboard Access: Reading clipboard without user knowledge
• Contact/Calendar Access: Uploading full contact lists unnecessarily
• Analytics Overreach: Tracking user behavior beyond stated purpose
• PII in Logs: Logging personally identifiable information
• Identifier Persistence: Using permanent device IDs for tracking
• No Privacy Controls: Missing opt-out mechanisms
• Data Minimization Failure: Collecting more data than needed
• Third-party SDK Leaks: SDKs transmitting user data without disclosure

Finding the Flag:

1. Tap "Load Sample Image" to load the preloaded photo
2. Tap "Analyze Metadata" to view all EXIF data
3. Look for the Image Description field in the metadata
4. The flag is hidden in one of the EXIF tags

EXIF Tags to Check:
• TAG_IMAGE_DESCRIPTION
• TAG_USER_COMMENT
• TAG_ARTIST
• TAG_MAKE
• TAG_MODEL
• TAG_GPS_LATITUDE
• TAG_GPS_LONGITUDE
• TAG_DATETIME

The flag format is: OWASP{...}

Privacy Protection Best Practices:

• Strip Metadata: Remove EXIF data before sharing images
• Data Minimization: Only collect data necessary for functionality
• User Consent: Explicit opt-in for data collection
• Privacy Settings: Provide granular privacy controls
• Anonymization: Remove PII from analytics data
• Secure Storage: Encrypt sensitive data at rest
• Access Controls: Restrict data access to necessary components
• Transparency: Clear privacy policy explaining data use
• Regular Audits: Periodically review data collection practices
• SDK Vetting: Evaluate third-party SDKs for privacy compliance

Implementation:
• Use ExifInterface to strip metadata
• Request minimum necessary permissions
• Implement privacy-by-design principles
• Provide data deletion mechanisms
• Respect system privacy settings

Client-side injection vulnerabilities occur when mobile applications don\'t properly sanitize user input before using it in SQL queries, JavaScript execution, or other interpreters. This lesson focuses on SQL injection in client-side SQLite databases.\n\nLearn how attackers manipulate SQL queries to bypass authentication, extract sensitive data, and compromise application security.

Client-Side Injection occurs when mobile applications fail to properly validate and sanitize user input before using it in SQL queries, JavaScript contexts, or other interpreters on the device.

Types of Client-Side Injection:

• SQL Injection in SQLite databases
• JavaScript injection in WebViews
• XML/JSON injection in parsers
• Command injection in system calls
• NoSQL injection in local databases
• File path injection

SQL Injection is particularly dangerous because:
• SQLite databases store sensitive app data
• Attackers can read any table
• Authentication can be bypassed
• Data can be modified or deleted
• Business logic can be circumvented

SQL Injection Vulnerabilities:

• String Concatenation: Building queries with user input
 - "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + input + "'"
 - Allows injection: ' OR 1=1--

• Improper Escaping: Not handling special characters
 - Single quotes (')
 - Comment markers (-- or /**/)
 - SQL keywords (OR, UNION, SELECT)

• Lack of Validation: Accepting any user input
 - No input length limits
 - No character whitelisting
 - No pattern matching

Common Attack Patterns:
• Authentication Bypass: ' OR '1'='1
• UNION Attacks: ' UNION SELECT * FROM secrets--
• Comment Injection: admin'--
• Always True Conditions: 1' OR '1'='1

SQL Injection Tips:

1. Start with simple tests:
 - Try a single quote (')
 - Look for SQL errors

2. Test for vulnerability:
 - Input: ' OR '1'='1
 - This makes the query always true

3. Extract all users:
 - Input: %' OR '1'='1
 - Shows all records in the table

4. Find hidden data:
 - Look for admin users
 - Check the full_name field
 - The flag is in an admin account

5. Successful injection signs:
 - Unexpected results returned
 - More data than expected
 - Different behavior than normal

Example Query:
SELECT * FROM users WHERE username LIKE '%INJECTION%'

Secure Coding Practices:

• Use Parameterized Queries:
 String[] args = {userInput};
 db.rawQuery("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?", args);

• Input Validation:
 - Whitelist allowed characters
 - Limit input length
 - Use regex patterns
 - Reject special SQL characters

• Prepared Statements:
 SQLiteStatement stmt = db.compileStatement(
 "INSERT INTO users VALUES (?, ?, ?)");
 stmt.bindString(1, username);

• Principle of Least Privilege:
 - Limit database permissions
 - Use separate accounts for different functions
 - Don't run as admin

• Content Providers:
 - Use Android Content Providers
 - Built-in parameterization
 - Proper escaping handled automatically

• Defense in Depth:
 - Validate on input
 - Parameterize queries
 - Limit error messages
 - Log suspicious activity
 - Regular security testing
Exploit SQL injection in a login form to bypass authentication and retrieve the admin password.\n\nGoal: Use SQL injection to login as admin and discover the hidden flag (admin password).

This challenge features a vulnerable login system that builds SQL queries using string concatenation. The application stores user accounts in a SQLite database with usernames, passwords, roles, and balance information.

Your Objective:
1. Identify the SQL injection vulnerability
2. Bypass the authentication mechanism
3. Retrieve the admin account password
4. Submit the password as the flag

The vulnerability exists because user input is directly concatenated into SQL queries without proper validation or parameterization.

Vulnerable Code Pattern:

String query = "SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE username = '" + username + "' AND password = '" + password + "'";

This allows attackers to:
• Break out of the query context
• Inject their own SQL logic
• Bypass authentication checks
• Retrieve data from any user

Example Attack:
Username: admin'--
Password: (anything)

Resulting Query:
SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE username = 'admin'--' AND password = '....'

The -- comments out the password check!

Attack Strategy:

1. Test for SQL Injection:
 Username: test'
 Password: test
 → If you see an error, it's vulnerable!

2. Bypass Authentication:
 Username: ' OR '1'='1
 Password: ' OR '1'='1
 → This makes the query always true

3. Target Specific User:
 Username: admin'--
 Password: (anything)
 → Comments out password check

4. Alternative Method:
 Username: ' OR username='admin
 Password: ' OR '1'='1
 → Specifically targets admin user

5. Look for the password field in the results
 → The flag is the admin's password!

The flag format matches the admin password in the database.

Prevention Techniques:

• Parameterized Queries:
 String[] selectionArgs = {username, password};
 Cursor cursor = db.query("accounts", 
 null, 
 "username = ? AND password = ?", 
 selectionArgs, 
 null, null, null);

• Input Sanitization:
 - Whitelist alphanumeric characters
 - Reject special characters: ' " -- ; /* */
 - Limit input length
 - Use regex validation

• Prepared Statements:
 PreparedStatement pstmt = connection.prepareStatement(
 "SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE username = ? AND password = ?");
 pstmt.setString(1, username);
 pstmt.setString(2, password);

• Hash Passwords:
 - Never store plaintext passwords
 - Use bcrypt or Argon2
 - Add salt to prevent rainbow tables
 - Compare hashes, not plaintext

• Error Handling:
 - Don't reveal database structure
 - Generic error messages
 - Log detailed errors server-side only
Search the product database. Can you discover the hidden \'secrets\' table and extract the admin token?

This challenge presents a product search feature with SQL injection vulnerability. Unlike simple authentication bypass, you need to use UNION-based injection to query a completely different table.

Database Structure:
• products table: name, category, price, stock
• secrets table: secret_key, secret_value (HIDDEN)

Your Objective:
1. Identify the number of columns in the products query
2. Use UNION SELECT to query the secrets table
3. Extract the admin_token value
4. Submit it as the flag

This requires understanding:
• UNION SQL operator
• Column count matching
• Cross-table data extraction

Vulnerable Code:

String query = "SELECT name, category, price, stock FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%" + input + "%'";

UNION-Based Injection allows:
• Combining results from multiple queries
• Accessing tables not in original query
• Bypassing application logic
• Extracting data from hidden tables

Attack Requirements:
1. Match column count in UNION
2. Match data types (use NULL for unknowns)
3. Terminate original query properly
4. Know or guess target table name

Example Attack:
' UNION SELECT secret_key, secret_value, NULL, NULL FROM secrets--

UNION Injection Strategy:

1. Find Column Count:
 Try: ' ORDER BY 4--
 If it works, there are 4+ columns
 If it fails, try ORDER BY 3, 2, etc.

2. Test UNION Compatibility:
 Input: ' UNION SELECT NULL,NULL,NULL,NULL--
 Adjust NULLs to match column count

3. Extract from Secrets Table:
 Input: ' UNION SELECT secret_key, secret_value, NULL, NULL FROM secrets--
 
 This retrieves all data from the hidden secrets table!

4. Alternative if table name unknown:
 Input: ' UNION SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table'--
 (Lists all tables in the database)

5. The admin_token secret_value is the flag

Note: The comment -- is crucial to ignore the rest of the query!

Advanced SQL Injection Prevention:

• ORM Usage:
 Use Room Persistence Library or ORM frameworks
 - Automatic parameterization
 - Type-safe queries
 - Compile-time verification

• Content Provider Security:
 @Override
 public Cursor query(Uri uri, String[] projection, 
 String selection, String[] selectionArgs, 
 String sortOrder) {
 // Use selectionArgs, never concatenate selection
 return db.query(table, projection, selection, 
 selectionArgs, null, null, sortOrder);
 }

• Query Builders:
 SQLiteQueryBuilder builder = new SQLiteQueryBuilder();
 builder.setTables("products");
 Cursor cursor = builder.query(db, projection, 
 selection, selectionArgs, null, null, sortOrder);

• Database Encryption:
 - Use SQLCipher for Android
 - Encrypt database files
 - Protect against device compromise

• Principle of Least Privilege:
 - Create separate database users
 - Limit table access per user
 - Use views to restrict columns
 - Deny UNION, subqueries if possible
